event: Before dawn on Day 24, Wren's palms on the threshold stone feel its hum lean south-southeast.
The thirty-second dawn vibration comes and fades; the directional emphasis remains.
It is the bearing the compass found on Day 19 and the Eye has watched since Day 6.
She journals: 'Day 24. Six. Stone signature directional, SSE. Going to look.'
At the fire she tells the others: something south-southeast, and the stone pointed.
'Hearthstone,' Theron says: a bigger settlement where the Greenwater bends round limestone.
His grandmother called it the ruin on the ridge; the ridge is three or four hours south.
Brecca freezes mid-tear: twenty-four days here and Wren has not looked south.
'I was looking at the stone.' 'For twenty-four days.' 'The stone was doing things.'
'So you are going south. Today.' 'Today,' Wren says, deciding as she says it.
Theron will stay: 'Someone should be here.'
Hadley, rolling his bedroll, will make the Millhaven run for supplies and to tell Maret.
Wren, who had not thought of Maret Osk in days, says: 'Invite her. Tell her about the stone.'
Hadley leaves north for the two-day walk to Millhaven.
Brecca, trowel in hand, announces she is coming: she wants to see what is out there.
Wren thinks of going alone, then of her mother's letter: 'Bring water. Wear heavy boots.'
At mid-morning Wren and Brecca leave south through the ghost-elm perimeter.
South of the ring the forest is older and denser, perhaps unwalked for three centuries.
Outside the perimeter the compass's south-southeast pull resolves clearer.
Wren crouches, palm to earth, and feels the [Foundation Stone] signature running south in the rock.
Brecca presses her hand down too: like a floor when someone walks in the room below.
'Okay,' Brecca says. 'That is new.' They walk.
After a mile the ghost-elms vanish into dense old oak and birch.
Brecca walks fast but sure-footed; Wren tells her 'Slower' twice.
'You walk like you are counting something.' Wren counts steps, grades, trees, deviations.
Brecca asks what the trees look like to her. 'Trees.' Brecca laughs, scattering a bird.
'Not everything has to be connected to a stone to be interesting.' Wren has no answer.
Ghost-elms return, singles then clusters, till the light turns grey-green.
These are larger and irregular, layering many harmonics; Wren stops: 'Listen.'
Brecca hears it: 'It hums. Different from the ones at the settlement.'
Wren's hand on a trunk: these are wild, resonating before anyone planted a ward.
Palm to the roots, she feels stone and tree signals interleaved, running south.
A discovery logs the wild ghost-elm grove: +45 XP, Surveying to 57.

changes.note: Discovery: wild ghost-elm grove, harmonics interleaved with the limestone

event: 'I could have told you that.' 'It knew I noticed.' 'Same thing. Different data.'
They walk on through the grove, and Wren notices its beauty without filing it.
The limestone surfaces in a ridge; the ghost-elms stop at its base and they climb.
Brecca's palms on the rock: same stone, same chisel tradition; someone dressed this face.
They reach the bare, wind-scoured crest in mid-afternoon.
South, the Greenwater curves round a limestone shelf ringed by large ghost-elms.
Through the canopy she sees walls, rooflines grown through, a clearing at the center.
It is a settlement built for hundreds where Varethen was built for dozens.
The compass now points straight south, a strong pull: this place has something to show her.
'A settlement. Bigger than Varethen.' Not today: it is two hours each way.
'Everything is a survey.' 'Some things are a survey because they should be.'
The same stone thread runs under the ridge: Varethen was not alone, it was part of something.
Wren reasons the tradition came from somewhere bigger than fourteen families.
Brecca reads the distant walls: thick, tighter coursing. 'That is not a village. That is a town.'
Wren sits, palms on the warm ridge rock, feeling the old thread between the two places.
They sit an hour; Wren surveys from the vantage while Brecca, for once, is quiet.
'Theron should see this. He will lose his mind. He pours tea slower.'
Wren laughs: in three days Brecca reads Theron better than she did in three weeks.
'We should go.' Brecca wants to see it up close; Wren wants Theron and two days of supplies.
They turn north; the pull sits behind her now, saying you saw it, now come back.
The threshold stone's signature grows with each step; she thinks the word home.
They pass back through the perimeter's ward-line hum and the bond network settles around her.
At dusk Theron looks up from the drainage channel and sees their faces.
'A settlement. South. On the river. On the same limestone.' Theron stands and looks south.
Brecca says a hundred meters across at least, thick walls, dressed stone throughout.
Theron sits at the fire and pours his tea slowly; Wren and Brecca exchange a look.
His grandmother said the families came from the south, from somewhere long empty.
Wren plans two days there and back once Hadley returns; Theron is coming. 'All of us.'
After the fire Wren sits at the threshold stone; its hum is omnidirectional again.
She journals the scouting: a settlement larger than Varethen, same formation. 'Varethen was not alone.'
She writes: 'Twelve days to the next pulse. The stone held last time. Will it hold again?'
She leaves the question unanswered; one data point is not a pattern.
At dawn on Day 25 she writes 'Day 25. Seven.' with the vibration in her palms.
Brecca is at the west wall, Theron at the channel, Hadley on the trail north.
The compass points south; the world is bigger than she knew, and she is going to see it.
